item.title: Magnuson-Stevens Fishery Conservation and Management Act Provisions; Fisheries of the Northeastern United States; Northeast Multispecies Fishery; Framework Adjustment 72
item.description: NMFS issues this interim final rule to implement Framework Adjustment 72 (Framework 72) to the Northeast Multispecies Fishery Management Plan (FMP), specifically to implement status determination criteria for Georges Bank yellowtail flounder, set catch limits for multispecies (groundfish) stocks, and revise the process for setting recreational measures for Atlantic cod and haddock. This action is necessary to respond to updated scientific information and to achieve the goals and objectives of the FMP. The measures are intended to help prevent overfishing, rebuild overfished stocks, achieve optimum yield, and ensure that management measures are based on the best scientific information available.

item.title: Response to Clean Air Act Section 176A Petition From New Hampshire
item.description: The Environmental Protection Agency (EPA) is proposing to grant a Clean Air Act (CAA or Act) petition submitted by the state of New Hampshire on December 24, 2025. The petition requests that the EPA remove the State of New Hampshire from the Ozone Transport Region (OTR) based on New Hampshire's continued attainment of the ozone National Ambient Air Quality Standards (NAAQS) and technical analyses demonstrating that the additional control of emissions from the state will not significantly contribute to ozone attainment in any area in the OTR. The OTR was established by the 1990 Clean Air Act Amendments and included the States of Connecticut, Delaware, Maine, Maryland, Massachusetts, New Hampshire, New Jersey, New York, Pennsylvania, Rhode Island, Vermont, the District of Columbia, and portions of northern Virginia.

Maine's Fall Foliage Season Set to Begin with Weekly Reports, New Event Feature

August 24, 2026

First 2026 foliage report arrives September 9; communities and organizations invited to share fall events with foliage visitors

Augusta, MAINE - One of Maine's most anticipated seasons is just around the corner, bringing brilliant color, harvest traditions, and countless reasons to explore the state.

The Maine Department of Agriculture, Conservation and Forestry (DACF) will launch its 2026 fall foliage reporting season on Wednesday, September 9, at MaineFoliage.com and by email to subscribers. Reports will be issued each Wednesday throughout the season, tracking the progression of fall color from northern Maine and higher elevations southward toward the coast.

This year, DACF is adding another way to help residents and visitors experience fall in Maine: organizations, communities, and event organizers are invited to submit fall events for consideration for inclusion in the weekly foliage reports.

"Fall foliage is more than something to see, it's an invitation to experience Maine," said DACF Commissioner Amanda Beal. "Whether that means visiting a farm, hiking a trail, attending a harvest festival, exploring a downtown, or simply following a scenic by-way, our weekly reports help people follow the color and discover more of Maine along the way."

2026 Fall Foliage Season Preview

DACF Maine Forest Service experts expect peak fall foliage to develop along its typical progression from north to south, with trees at higher elevations generally developing color before those at lower elevations.

Maine's tremendous diversity of tree species, landscapes, and growing conditions helps create both its spectacular fall color and an extended viewing season. Northern and coastal areas offer striking contrasts between evergreens and colorful maples, birches, and oaks, while inland forests provide a broad palette of fall color set among Maine's abundant lakes, rivers, mountains, and working landscapes.

While foliage conditions can vary from one location to another, Maine's healthy and diverse forests continue to provide outstanding opportunities for fall color.

"The great thing about fall foliage in Maine is that there isn't just one place or one moment to experience it," said MFS Director and State Forester Patty Cormier. "Color develops at different times across the state and across different landscapes. If conditions aren't at their best in one location, spectacular foliage is often just down the road."

Fall color develops through a combination of shorter daylight, cooler temperatures, leaf pigments, moisture, and other environmental conditions. As days shorten, trees slow their production of chlorophyll, revealing the yellow and orange pigments already present in leaves. Cooler temperatures and other environmental factors can also influence the red and purple colors associated with anthocyanin pigments.

Because Maine's forests contain such a diverse mix of tree species and growing conditions, the result is a constantly changing mosaic of color throughout the season.

New: Share Your Fall Event with Maine Foliage Visitors

For 2026, DACF is inviting organizations, communities, farms, nonprofits, municipalities, and event organizers to submit public fall events for possible inclusion in Maine's Weekly Foliage Reports. DACF is looking for more activities that give residents and visitors another reason to get out and experience autumn in Maine, including:

  • Harvest festivals and agricultural fairs
  • Farm and food events
  • Outdoor recreation and nature-based activities
  • Arts and cultural events
  • Community festivals and celebrations
  • Other public events that complement the fall foliage experience

Events should take place during Maine's fall foliage reporting season, generally mid-September through mid-October, and must be open to the public.

SUBMIT YOUR FALL EVENT

DACF will review events based on timing, location, relevance to the foliage season, and available space. Submitted information may be edited for length, clarity, and style.

Follow the Color at MaineFoliage.com

Throughout the season, MaineFoliage.com is the official resource for tracking Maine's changing fall color. Weekly reports provide foliage conditions across the state and help residents and visitors decide when and where to explore. The first report will be published on Wednesday, September 9, 2026, with updated reports following every Wednesday through the foliage season.

From Maine's northern forests and western mountains to its lakes, farms, downtowns, and coast, there is no single way to experience fall in Maine. Following the changing color and exploring the places, people, events, and landscapes along the way is part of what makes the season special.

About Maine's Fall Foliage Reports

For 68 years, the DACF has produced Maine's official fall foliage reports, drawing on observations from forestry and conservation professionals across the state. Published weekly throughout the season, the reports track the progression of color and leaf drop across seven foliage zones and provide information and resources to help residents and visitors make the most of Maine's spectacular fall season.

Maine DEP Initiates Legal Action Against Mallinckrodt US LLC to Address Cleanup Failures at Orrington Site

Maine Department of Environmental Protection sent this bulletin at 08/25/2026 03:45 PM EDT

--- PRESS RELEASE ---

For Immediate Release

 

Maine DEP Initiates Legal Action Against Mallinckrodt US LLC to Address Cleanup Failures at Orrington Site

 

AUGUSTA, August 25, 2026 — The Department of Environmental Protection (DEP) filed a formal complaint today in Penobscot County Superior Court against Mallinckrodt US LLC (Mallinckrodt). The complaint details the failure by Mallinckrodt to complete cleanup of the former Holtrachem site located along the Penobscot River in Orrington, Maine, one of Maine’s most contaminated sites. Mallinckrodt has not met the remediation standards required in the DEP’s 2008 Designation of Uncontrolled Hazardous Substance Site and Order, that was affirmed in 2010 by the Board of Environmental Protection (BEP) in its own slightly modified order, affirmed in 2012 by the Maine Business and Consumer Docket, and finally affirmed in 2014 by the Maine Supreme Judicial Court sitting as the Law Court.

The former Holtrachem site was a chloralkali manufacturing facility, which made chemicals commonly used in the pulp and paper industry. Historic operations resulted in a significant amount of contamination, including highly toxic mercury and chloropicrin, in surrounding soils, groundwaters, and the Penobscot River. Site-specific standards were established by the DEP and BEP Orders to ensure that the site would be cleaned up in a manner that would protect public health, safety, and the environment.  Despite these Orders, large areas of soils still remain on site that exceed the site-specific cleanup standards.

The DEP has worked diligently to provide oversight during cleanup of the former Holtrachem site to ensure that Mallinckrodt conducts remediation in compliance with the DEP and BEP Orders. While progress has been made, it began to slow down as early as 2018 when Mallinckrodt began the first of several attempts to seek relief from meeting the Orders’ requirements. Since 2023, Mallinckrodt has ceased any meaningful progress toward remediation at the site.

Prior to today’s filing, two Notices of Violation (NOVs) were issued to Mallinckrodt on March 19, 2025, and October 22, 2025. These NOVs provide more detailed information about Mallinckrodt’s failure to comply with the DEP and BEP Orders. Copies of these NOVs are available on the DEP Mallinckrodt webpage.

The Department is seeking injunctive relief from the Penobscot Superior Court and civil penalties for ongoing violations.

WHEREAS, honey bees (Apis Mellifera) and other native insects are essential pollinators that contribute to food security by pollinating the plants we use and one-third of the food we consume; and

WHEREAS, honey bees face serious threats from many sources including pests and viruses, loss of habitat, toxic pesticide and herbicide usage, and changes in climate and resulting water patterns; and

WHEREAS, honey bees are essential in the production of Maine's heritage crops including blueberries and apples; and

WHEREAS, Maine's honey bees produce approximately 450,000 pounds of honey each year and contribute an estimated annual $100-150 million to the state’s economy; and

WHEREAS, Maine has almost 2,000 beekeepers ranging from hobbyists with as few as one hive, to part time business owners, to full time commercial beekeepers with thousands of hives; and

WHEREAS, while traditional beekeeping occurred in rural areas of Maine for the purpose of helping pollinate farm crops, beekeeping is now growing in urban areas as the result of rising numbers of hobby beekeepers interested in increasing biodiversity and local food production; and

WHEREAS, the State of Maine has an exemplary apiary inspection program for the protection of honey bees and education of beekeepers in the prevention and spread of apiary diseases and pests; and

WHEREAS, since 1975 the Honey Bee has been recognized as Maine's official state insect; and

WHEREAS, the Maine State Beekeepers Association is celebrating its 50th year of incorporation in 2026, and will host the annual “Bee Fest” on September 13 at the Viles Arboretum in Augusta;

NOW THEREFORE, be it resolved, that I, Janet T. Mills, Governor of the State of Maine do hereby proclaim September 13, 2026 as 

Maine Honey Bee Day

and I encourage all Maine people to join in recognizing the importance of honey bees to our state.

the Great Seal of the State to be

Bradbury Mountain State Park Selected as 2026 Leave No Trace Spotlight; Community Events Set for September 3-5

August 26, 2026

Three days of activities will bring together Leave No Trace, Maine State Parks, volunteers, and community partners to celebrate and care for one of Maine's treasured outdoor spaces.

Pownal - The Maine Department of Agriculture, Conservation and Forestry (DACF) announced today that Bradbury Mountain State Park in Pownal has been selected as a 2026 Leave No Trace Spotlight, bringing three days of community events, outdoor education, and hands-on stewardship to the park and surrounding area September 3-5, 2026.

"Bradbury Mountain is a place people return to again and again, to hike, bike, gather with family, take in the view, and enjoy being outside," said Chris Silsbee, Manager of Bradbury Mountain State Park. Being selected as a Leave No Trace Spotlight gives us a great opportunity to bring the community together, have some fun, and put stewardship into action. Whether you join us for trivia, sit around the campfire, or spend Saturday working on a trail, there's a way for everyone to be part of it.

Activities begin Thursday evening in Freeport and continue through Saturday at Bradbury Mountain State Park.

  • September 3, 2026: Leave No Trace Trivia Night
  • September 4, 2026: Fireside with the Ranger, Leave No Trace Staff & Hot Dog Roast
  • September 4, 2026: Leave No Trace Outreach Tent
  • September 5, 2026: Leave No Trace Event & Stewardship Project
  • September 5, 2026: Leave No Trace Stewardship Project

There is also a special incentive for early arrivals: the first 25 cars through the park gate whose driver says, "Bigfoot Leaves No Trace at Bradbury," will receive a gift bag featuring items from local event sponsors.

About the Leave No Trace Spotlight Program

Each year, Leave No Trace selects nominated outdoor areas for its Spotlight program, which brings communities together to care for and protect places people love to visit. Spotlights combine education, community outreach, and hands-on stewardship to help address impacts from outdoor recreation while giving visitors practical tools they can use long after the event ends. Bradbury Mountain State Park's Spotlight is supported by the Subaru/Leave No Trace Traveling Team, Maine State Parks, community volunteers, and local partners.

About Bradbury Mountain State Park

Bradbury Mountain State Park, located in Pownal, is one of Maine's original five state parks. The park offers more than 20 miles of trails for hiking, mountain biking, and horseback riding, along with camping and opportunities to experience the area's natural and cultural history. The summit of Bradbury Mountain provides expansive views and is a popular location for observing the annual migration of hawks and other birds of prey. For information about Bradbury Mountain State Park, visit the Maine State Parks website.

item.title: Federal judge blocks attempts to restrict mail-in voting
item.description: AUGUSTA, MAINE – A federal judge in Boston blocked the Trump administration from interfering with states’ rights to conduct mail-in voting for the upcoming November elections, now 67 days away. Judge Indira Talwani ruled yesterday that the plaintiffs were likely to succeed in proving the administration’s order was unconstitutional. “Last night’s decision was wonderful news for Maine voters who rely on absentee voting,” Secretary Bellows said . “The judge made clear that the states, not the federal government, are in charge of elections. That goes to the heart of our legal fights in court against the Trump Administration. We will continue to stand with other states and voting rights advocates across the nation to defend the voting rights – including the right to vote by mail – for every citizen.” In the decision, Judge Talwani wrote, “the Constitution charges the States with election administration” going on to say that no law has been passed by Congress that “would permit the USPS to regulate election mail.” The judge went even further to note that with just two months to the election, it would an expensive and likely impossible task for the 2026 election, saying, “Plaintiff States face irreparable harm where they are required to comply with a likely unconstitutional regulation for which compliance is practically impossible.” ### Attachment: read the 08-27-26 order

AUGUSTA, MAINE – A federal judge in Boston blocked the Trump administration from interfering with states’ rights to conduct mail-in voting for the upcoming November elections, now 67 days away. Judge Indira Talwani ruled yesterday that the plaintiffs were likely to succeed in proving the administration’s order was unconstitutional. 

“Last night’s decision was wonderful news for Maine voters who rely on absentee voting,” Secretary Bellows said. “The judge made clear that the states, not the federal government, are in charge of elections. That goes to the heart of our legal fights in court against the Trump Administration. We will continue to stand with other states and voting rights advocates across the nation to defend the voting rights – including the right to vote by mail – for every citizen.”

In the decision, Judge Talwani wrote, “the Constitution charges the States with election administration” going on to say that no law has been passed by Congress that “would permit the USPS to regulate election mail.” The judge went even further to note that with just two months to the election, it would an expensive and likely impossible task for the 2026 election, saying, “Plaintiff States face irreparable harm where they are required to comply with a likely unconstitutional regulation for which compliance is practically impossible.”

WHEREAS, Maine has a rich and storied tradition of hunting and angling that dates back further than the state itself and carries forward to this day; and


WHEREAS, hunting and angling continue to be an integral component of the cultural fabric of communities throughout the state, and over recent years have offered a growing number of participants an opportunity to connect with nature on a personal level while simultaneously providing food security, a sense of self-sufficiency, and both mental and physical health benefits; and

 
WHEREAS, Maine's sportsmen and women were among the first conservationists to support the establishment of the Maine Department of Inland Fisheries and Wildlife to conserve fish, wildlife and their habitat, and through their license fees helped fund state efforts to provide for healthy and sustainable natural resources; and


WHEREAS, upon realizing that license fees alone were insufficient to restore and sustain healthy fish and wildlife populations, sportsmen and women supported self-imposed excise taxes on firearms and ammunition, fishing tackle and motorboat fuels to raise additional conservation funds; and


WHEREAS, to this day, the Maine Department of Inland Fisheries and Wildlife is funded, in part, by sportsmen and women, through this American System of Conservation Funding – a “user pays - public benefits” approach that is widely recognized as the most successful model for funding fish and wildlife management in the world; and


WHEREAS, last year alone, Maine's sportsmen and women generated $32 million through this system to support the conservation efforts of the Maine Department of Inland Fisheries and Wildlife; and


WHEREAS, 548,194 hunters and anglers support the state's economy through their spending, contributing to the $3.9 billion spent on outdoor activities in Maine last year; 


NOW THEREFORE, be it resolved that I, Janet T. Mills, Governor of the State of Maine, do hereby proclaim September 26, 2026 as 

National Hunting and Fishing Day

in Maine, and I urge all citizens to recognize the many and varied social, cultural, economic, and ecological benefits of our time-honored traditions of hunting and angling.

In testimony whereof, I have caused

the Great Seal of the State to be

hereunto affixed GIVEN under my

hand at Augusta this twenty seventh day

item.title: Process for Authorizing Seasonal Migratory Game Bird Hunting
item.description: The U.S. Fish and Wildlife Service (Service or we) is changing the administrative process for authorizing seasonal migratory game bird hunting in the United States. Migratory game bird hunting regulations are currently promulgated annually to provide opportunities for recreation and sustenance; aid Federal, State, and Tribal governments in the management of migratory game birds; and allow harvests at levels compatible with migratory game bird population status and habitat conditions. The Service is adopting a more efficient administrative process for authorizing seasonal migratory game bird hunting. The Service will issue a memorandum to establish the limits and authorize seasonal migratory game bird hunting once every 3 years. The Service will continue to make annual decisions on harvest levels and will update the memorandum sooner than 3 years if changes are prescribed by our decision frameworks. The process eliminates the need for subsequent annual Federal regulation promulgation and rulemaking and is expected to increase efficiency; better meet State, Tribal, and Federal rulemaking constraints; and reduce the complexity and costs. Our goal is to better serve State partners and the hunting public while continuing to meet the legal and conservation purposes of the Migratory Bird Treaty Act. Tribes are already authorized under a similar process.

item.title: Updates to the National Pollutant Discharge Elimination System Definitions and Exclusions
item.description: The U.S. Environmental Protection Agency (EPA) proposes to revise a regulatory definition under the Clean Water Act (CWA) permitting regulations pertaining to discharges in the contiguous zone and ocean. The proposal would revise the regulatory definition of "discharge of a pollutant" to reflect and faithfully implement the statutory exclusion of vessels and other floating craft that add pollutants in the contiguous zone or the ocean from inclusion in the definition of "discharge of a pollutant" or "discharge", and thus, from National Pollutant Discharge Elimination System (NPDES) program requirements. The proposed rulemaking would also make conforming and clarifying changes to the NPDES regulatory exclusion for vessels and other floating craft. The effect of these changes would be that the addition of pollutants by a vessel or other floating craft in the contiguous zone or the ocean that is not secured to the seabed would not be a discharge and would not require CWA NPDES permit authorization to add pollutants to those waters.

DACF Invites Participation in the 2027 Maine Agricultural Trades Show

August 28, 2026

Businesses, organizations, educators, and service providers are encouraged to get involved and shape Maine's annual agricultural gathering

AUGUSTA - The Maine Department of Agriculture, Conservation and Forestry (DACF) is inviting businesses, farms, agricultural organizations, educators, researchers, service providers, and others connected to Maine agriculture, food systems, and natural resources to express interest in participating in the 2027 Maine Agricultural Trades Show, scheduled for January 12-14, 2027.

The annual show brings together Maines agricultural community for three days of exhibits, education, professional development, networking, and conversations about the opportunities and challenges facing agriculture and food systems.

DACF is encouraging both returning participants and organizations that have not previously participated to explore ways to become involved.

Many Ways to Participate

The Agricultural Trades Show offers several ways for businesses and organizations to connect with attendees and contribute to the program, including:

  • Exhibit booths for businesses and organizations offering agricultural services, supplies, tools, equipment, programs, and resources.
  • Conference sessions for workshops, annual meetings, continuing education, research and development updates, and discussions focused on agriculture, food systems, and natural resources.
  • The Maine Stage features approximately 40-minute programs designed for broad audience appeal, including farmer spotlights, demonstrations, interviews, and other presentations.
  • Room rentals for focus groups, competitions, meetings, and other agriculture-focused activities.
  • Sponsorship opportunities supporting show programming, hospitality, audiovisual services, and other activities.
  • The Listening Post, which provides opportunities for volunteer-led business coaching, networking, listening sessions, and other activities.

Organizations with ideas, including those that do not fit neatly into any of these categories, are encouraged to submit their interests and connect with show organizers. Questions may be directed to acfagtradesshow@maine.gov.

New Participants and New Ideas Encouraged

The Agricultural Trades Show serves a diverse agricultural community, and DACF is particularly interested in broadening awareness of opportunities to participate.

Farms and producers, agricultural businesses, commodity organizations, food-system partners, educators, researchers, conservation and natural resource organizations, financial and business service providers, workforce development organizations, and others whose work supports Maine agriculture are encouraged to consider how they could contribute.

The interest form is the first step. Submitting the form allows potential participants to identify the opportunities that interest them and provides show organizers with contact information for follow-up as planning progresses.

The priority deadline is September 23, 2026, for early consideration of exhibit space, conference sessions, and room rentals. Initial selection status notifications are expected by October 1. Interest forms will continue to be accepted and reviewed throughout fall 2026, with waitlist requests accepted until the show.

The Maine Agricultural Trades Show is an annual gathering of Maines agricultural community hosted by the Maine Department of Agriculture, Conservation and Forestry. The show connects farmers, producers, businesses, organizations, educators, service providers, and the public through exhibits, educational programming, networking, and opportunities to learn about Maine agriculture and the resources available to support it.

Annual Tea Celebrating Deaf Culture to Take Place September 17

The 35th annual tea and awards presentation will take place from 2 to 4 p.m. in the Hall of Flags

AUGUSTA, MAINE -In celebration of Deaf culture and the heritage of AmericanSign Language (ASL), as well as Deaf literature, art and folklore, Governor Janet Mills has issued a proclamation designating the week of Sept. 20-26, 2026, as Deaf Culture Week.

To kick off the week, the Commission for the Deaf, Hard of Hearing and Late Deafened will hold its 35th Annual Tea in Celebration of Deaf Culture Week on Sept. 17, from 2 to 4 p.m. at the Hall of Flags in the State House in Augusta. The event is open to the public.

Clayton Marr III will give the keynote address. Marr grew up in Westbrook and currently lives in Knoxville, Tenn. where he is the student activity coordinator for the Tennessee Schools for the Deaf. He works with Deaf students to support their academic success, personal growth, and independence.

"Maine's Deaf community has enriched our state for generations through its language, culture, traditions and contributions. I've proudly declared September 20-26 as Deaf Culture Week in celebration of that heritage and the Deaf and hard-of-hearing Mainers who make our state a better place," said Governor Mills.

"The Maine Department of Labor is proud to support the Commission for the Deaf, Hard of Hearing and Late Deafened and this 35th annual celebration of Deaf culture. I encourage Maine employers to harness the many skills and experiences of people with disabilities. DOL's Bureau of Rehabilitation Services is ready to assist workers and employers with vocational rehabilitation, training and support," said Commissioner Laura Fortman.

This year, the Commission will present seven awards to eight individuals and organizations that have contributed to Deaf culture in Maine.

Awards and their recipients are:

Promoting American Sign Language, Deaf Culture and Deaf People Award Lisa Penney, Donna Van Horn

Citizenship Youth Award Gavin Phelan

Ginny Hewes Advocate for the Needs of the Deaf Community Award Jennifer McCann, LCSW

Outstanding Citizenship Award Andrew Blethen

Outstanding Commendation Award Immigrant Legal Advocacy Project (ILAP)

Dr. Toni H. Rees Interpreter Award Cid Pollard

Clifton F. Rodgers Outstanding Service to the Deaf Community Award Sammy Hargis

Maine Heads to The Big E with Food, Farms, and Makers

September 3, 2026

The Maine Building at the Big E returns for 17 days of Maine food, farms, makers, and traditions, September 18 - October 4

AUGUSTA, Maine (September 3, 2026) - From loaded Maine baked potatoes and lobster rolls to wild blueberry crisp, maple milkshakes, smoked salmon, and wood-fired pizza featuring Maine ingredients, the tastes and traditions of Maine are returning to The Big E this fall.

The State of Maine Building, located on the Avenue of States alongside buildings representing the five other New England states, will welcome visitors throughout the 17-day Eastern States Exposition, September 18 through October 4, 2026, in West Springfield, Massachusetts. Maine Day will be celebrated on Saturday, September 19.

For more than a century, the Maine Building has introduced generations of fairgoers to the people, products, and traditions that make Maine stand apart. The Maine Department of Agriculture, Conservation and Forestry (DACF) owns and operates the building as a showcase for Maine agriculture, food, fisheries, forests, tourism, artisans, and businesses.

"The Big E gives Maine a special opportunity to showcase our food, farms, and agricultural businesses to people from across New England and beyond," said DACF Commissioner Amanda Beal. "Food is one of the most immediate and memorable ways to make that connection. Someone may come into the Maine Building for a baked potato, lobster roll, or a maple or wild blueberry dish, but they leave with a greater appreciation for the farmers, producers, and small businesses behind those products."

The Big E is one of the largest fairs in North America, providing Maine businesses with access to an enormous regional marketplace. For exhibiting producers and makers, the opportunity extends beyond sales during the fair, helping introduce their products to new customers and build awareness that can lead to future visits, online purchases, and other business opportunities.

"We view the Big E as both a marketplace and a long-term opportunity to build awareness of Maine agriculture," said DACF Bureau of Agriculture, Food and Rural Resources Director Craig Lapine. "Many of Maine's farms and food businesses are small businesses, and reaching an audience of this scale is difficult to accomplish individually. By bringing them together in the Maine Building, we can show visitors the robust diversity of what Maine grows, harvests, makes and creates."

Taste Maine at The Big E

Food remains one of the biggest draws at the Maine Building, and the 2026 lineup offers fairgoers plenty of ways to experience Maine.

Longtime favorites include the Maine Potato Board's iconic loaded baked potatoes and Maine lobster rolls. Tree of Life Maple Farm will offer organic Maine maple syrup, maple cream, candy, cotton candy, coffee, and milkshakes, while Valley View Orchard Pies brings fruit pies, whoopie pies, and other baked goods from its Oxford bakery.

Maine aquaculture is also on the menu, with the Maine Aquaculture Association offering smoked salmon while introducing visitors to Maine's growing aquaculture sector and the Maine Oyster Trail.

This year's offerings also highlight collaborations among Maine farms and food businesses.

Fields Fields Blueberries, a woman-owned organic wild blueberry farm in Dresden, will serve its renowned wild blueberry crisp topped with Maine-made Gifford's ice cream.

QP Burger Food Truck will bring together products from multiple Maine businesses in its burgers, hot dogs, and sides, including Fox Family Potato Chips, Raye's Mustard, and Morse's sauerkraut.

Fire & Company Catering will showcase Maine flavors through wood-fired pizza and beverages featuring Maine producers and ingredients.

"These collaborations tell an important story about Maine's food economy," Beal said. "When Maine farms, food producers, and businesses use and promote one another's products, the benefit reaches beyond a single business. Visitors get a great Maine experience while seeing firsthand how interconnected our agricultural and food community can be."

More Than Food

The Maine Building experience extends well beyond the menu.

Visitors can shop for Maine-made wood products, jewelry, personal-care products, artisan goods, and gifts. Dailey Woodworking and Friends will feature work from more than a dozen Maine makers, alongside longtime and returning exhibitors including Ledgeway Farm, MARTINI Jewels, Sider's Woodcrafting, Sunshine Apothecary, and Winter Whimsies.

Short-term exhibitors rotating through the building include Maine authors and makers, Liberty Graphics, Pussums Cat Company, Sweet Monkey Business, and West Maquoit Vinegar Works.

The Maine Flower Collective will greet visitors with a display of Maine-grown dried flowers highlighting the state's flower farmers and florists, while the Maine Forest and Logging Museum will help tell the story of Maine's forestry heritage.

The Maine Office of Tourism will also be on hand, along with the Maine Tourism Association, to help visitors discover Maine destinations and experiences.

"Our goal is to spark a connection with Maine that inspires a visit to our state for culinary experiences," said Maine Office of Tourism Director Carolann Ouellette. "The Maine-made products on exhibit at the Big E all tell a story that is shaped by the landscape and culture of Maine. When fair attendees discover a Maine product, they get to learn about the farm and people behind the product, and that develops a bond that we hope will carry forward in a trip to Maine's farms and food businesses.

Mills, Governor of the State of Maine, do hereby proclaim the week of September 28-October 4, 2026, as Maine Wasted Food Prevention Week and I encourage all Maine people to become aware of the wasted food in our homes, schools and all around us, and to commit to stop throwing food away. WHEREAS, food is one of Maine’s most valuable resources and is essential for the health and nutrition of all our 1.4 million residents; and

WHEREAS, nearly 40 percent of food produced in Maine is never eaten – over 361,000 tons annually – primarily ending up in landfills where it produces dangerous methane gas which is 28 times more potent than carbon dioxide and a major contributor to climate change; and

WHEREAS, Maine people can save money by preventing wasted food, with the average Maine family spending nearly $3,000 annually on food that is thrown away; and

WHEREAS, over 80 percent of consumers misunderstand food date labels causing large amounts of perfectly good food to be thrown away in homes, businesses, and even food pantries; and

WHEREAS, Maine communities can substantially reduce their waste disposal costs by preventing wasted food since food is the single largest municipal solid waste component; and

WHEREAS, Maine K-12 schools have a special role in educating our next generation to reduce, recover, and recycle the estimated 7 million pounds of school food wasted annually; and

WHEREAS, we can help our farmers, strengthen our local food systems, and conserve our natural resources – water, air, energy, and land – by valuing Maine food and composting food scraps instead of wasting it as trash; 

NOW THEREFORE, be it resolved that I, Janet T. Mills, Governor of the State of Maine, do hereby proclaim the week of September 28-October 4, 2026, as

Maine Wasted Food Prevention Week

and I encourage all Maine people to become aware of the wasted food in our homes, schools and all around us, and to commit to stop throwing food away.

hereunto affixed GIVEN under my 
hand at Augusta this second day
